topBuzzwords.definition: French 'Sécurité' splits in English: Safety = protection from unintentional hazards and system failures; Security = protection against intentional threats, unlawful acts, and terrorism.
Landside = public areas before security (check-in, arrivals hall). Airside = strictly secured operations areas beyond security (gates, apron, taxiways, runways).
Concourse = large, open public hall where passengers circulate and relax. Bottleneck = narrow transit corridor or checkpoint causing localized movement congestion.
Dwell time = elapsed time passengers spend in the terminal between security screening and boarding. Reduced via automated bag drop, e-gates, CT scanners, and facial recognition.
The designated paved area where aircraft park at designated stands to board/deboard, refuel, load baggage, and undergo ground servicing (called 'Ramp' in the US, 'Apron' in the UK).
Essential communicative collocations: to book a flight, to board a plane, to check in, to clear customs, and to travel with carry-on luggage.
GPU (Ground Power Unit) = mobile ground generator supplying electricity at the gate. APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) = small gas turbine in the aircraft tail used when engines and GPU are off.

topBuzzwords.term: Travel Idioms (Scenic Route, Hit the Road)
topBuzzwords.definition: Conversational storytelling idioms: to hit the road (depart), to take the scenic route (longer picturesque path), and to be in the driver's seat (in control).
TRC = Turnaround Coordinator supervising ramp tasks between flight arrival and departure. AODB = Airport Operational Database managing flight schedules, gate changes, and allocated stands.
A traveler who refuses to follow crew instructions or behaves disruptively, risking flight diversions, police arrest, and heavy airline costs.
LCC = budget airline offering cheap baseline tickets. Ancillary Revenue = extra income from non-ticket sales (carry-on bags, seat selection, on-board meals).

topBuzzwords.term: Get Off to a Flying Start & Word of Mouth
topBuzzwords.definition: Get off to a flying start = beginning a semester or project with immediate success and momentum. Word of mouth = organic communication from person to person.
Direct flight = keeps the same single flight number but may include intermediate tech stops. Non-stop flight = flies between origin and destination with zero stops.
When an airline sells more tickets than available seats in anticipation of no-shows, risking involuntary denied boarding and statutory compensation obligations.

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 🛡️ Safety vs. Security in English
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: French 'Sécurité' splits into two distinct operational English terms. Never confuse them: 'Safety' prevents unintentional accidents and hazards; 'Security' protects against intentional human threats and attacks.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "Aviation safety deals with bird strikes and de-icing; aviation security handles passenger screening, CT scanners, and hijackings."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ❌ 'Luggages' and 'Trainings' do NOT exist!
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Both 'luggage' and 'training' are uncountable nouns in English. Never add an 's'. Use 'pieces of luggage' or 'training courses'.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "We checked three pieces of luggage and completed our training course on ramp safety."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 📍 Spatial Prepositions: At vs. In vs. On vs. Through
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Use 'at' for specific nodes and facilities (at the gate, at the checkpoint), 'in' for enclosed spaces (in the concourse, in the cabin), 'on' for pavement surfaces (on the apron, on Runway 14L), and 'through/along' for movement.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "Passengers wait in the concourse, board at gate 12, walk along the jet bridge, while the aircraft holds on taxiway Bravo."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 🗣️ Pronunciation Trap: Alternate (Verb vs. Noun)
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Word stress changes with grammatical function: the verb 'to alternate' is stressed /ˈɔːl.tər.neɪt/, but the noun/adjective 'an alternate airport' is pronounced /ɔːlˈtɜː.nət/.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "If weather drops below minimums at Toulouse, the captain will divert to an alternate airport."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 🗣️ Pronunciation Trap: Itinerary
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Multiple students flagged pronunciation difficulty with 'itinerary'. Stress is on the second syllable: /aɪˈtɪn.ər.ər.i/ (eye-TIN-er-uh-ree).
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "Could you please confirm our flight itinerary before we head to the boarding gate?"

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ⏱️ Reported Speech Backshift & Time References
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: When reporting past dialogue, tenses shift back (present -> past, past -> past perfect; will -> would), and time adverbs shift ('today' -> 'that day', 'yesterday' -> 'the day before', 'tomorrow' -> 'the following day').
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "He said he was running on empty that day and would take the train the following morning."

strengths: Rapid grasp of the crucial operational distinction between Safety (unintentional hazards) and Security (intentional threats).
Fast adoption of modern aerodrome and terminal infrastructure terminology (Concourse, Jet Bridge, Apron, Stands, GPU, Dwell Time).
Active use of travel collocations, idioms, and reported speech backshifting in communicative peer simulations.
growthAreas: Spatial Preposition Accuracy: Mastering 'at' (nodes), 'in' (spaces), and 'on' (pavement surfaces) during real-time spoken descriptions.
Spoken Fluency & Hesitation: Reducing pauses and sentence-building delays when searching for specialized English nouns.
Pronunciation Phonetics: Drilling vowel sounds and word stress in tricky multi-syllable terms ('itinerary', 'alternate', 'throughout').
cohortReflections.feAdvice: Students strongly emphasize that knowing aerodrome zones (airside, landside, concourse, apron, holding points) and using precise prepositions ('on the apron', 'at the gate', 'in the concourse') gives immediate authority and fluency during the 30-minute Formative Evaluation.

verbatimQuotes.quote: We talked mostly about security and safety and I was surprised to discover the difference with the French words since 'Sécurité' doesn't mean 'Security' but 'Safety'. Today we also talked about prepositions: 'in' when it's in an enclosed space, 'at' when it's a specific location, and 'on' when it's on a surface.
verbatimQuotes.takeaway: Mastering the Safety/Security distinction and spatial prepositions prevents operational ambiguity.

verbatimQuotes.quote: During our airport presentation, this vocabulary will help me explain where I am at any point: from the concourse to the gates, the apron with the different runways and taxiways... all while using the correct preposition. I'm sure that learning all this vocab will go a long way concerning our fluency.
verbatimQuotes.takeaway: Mental mapping of the airport infrastructure drives fluent spoken delivery.

verbatimQuotes.quote: Testing myself with the TOEIC questions in here as well as on GlobalExam is a funnier way to incorporate the information in my brain than the old way of learning by heart with a copybook. Discussion skills worked in pairs surely are unavoidable to make a great formative evaluation.
verbatimQuotes.takeaway: Interactive daily quizzing and peer dialogue outperform rote memorization.

verbatimQuotes.quote: My main problem is fluency because I am always looking for a word when talking to someone. I also need some time to build my sentences, so I think that I have to talk as much as possible to improve on these points.
verbatimQuotes.takeaway: Regular communicative pairwork reduces hesitation and builds sentence speed.
